growth_story.headline: Sweden's income per person grew 3.0 percent a year in 1998–2007, then just 0.6 percent a year since 2008 as productivity growth faded and shocks hit.
growth_story.arc: Sweden's income per person grew 0.6 percent a year in 1990–1997, an era that opened with falls in 1991, 1992 and 1993 (the worst was 2.6 percent in 1993) before growth returned in 1994. From 1998 to 2007 growth ran at 3.0 percent a year; the IMF says reforms of the late 1980s and early 1990s that strengthened competition led to strong productivity growth until the global financial crisis, and Sweden was an early leader in information technology. Since 2008 growth has averaged 0.6 percent a year: income per person fell 5.1 percent in 2009 during the global financial crisis, and the IMF describes a lasting decline in productivity growth since then. The pandemic cut income per person by 2.6 percent in 2020 before a 4.6 percent rebound in 2021. Inflation then reached 8.4 percent in 2022 and 8.5 percent in 2023, income per person fell 0.7 percent in 2023, and the IMF links weak activity in 2024 to lower real incomes, much variable-rate debt and the tight policy used to bring inflation down. Growth over 2016–2025 averaged 0.7 percent a year, down from 1.1 over 2006–2015 and below the structural-peer median of 1.4, though income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025.

threads.title: Reforms and the IT boom
threads.text: Reforms in the late 1980s and early 1990s strengthened competition and, the IMF says, led to strong productivity growth until the global financial crisis. Sweden was ahead of many rich countries in information technology, and in the 1990s new firms replacing less productive ones drove productivity gains. This was the backdrop to growth of 3.0 percent a year in 1998–2007.

threads.title: Productivity slows after 2008
threads.text: Output per worker in Sweden is among the highest in Europe, but its growth has slowed since the global financial crisis. The IMF finds that established firms now drive most productivity gains rather than new firms replacing old ones, and that work hours have shifted toward slower-growing sectors such as construction.

threads.title: Inflation, interest rates and housing
threads.text: Inflation reached 8.4 percent in 2022 and 8.5 percent in 2023. The IMF says lower real incomes, a high share of variable-rate mortgages and the tight policy needed to bring inflation down kept activity subdued in 2024, while house prices fell for a second year. Income per person fell 0.7 percent in 2023 and grew 0.7 percent in 2024.

threads.text: The IMF expects an ageing population and slower population growth than in the previous decade to hold down how fast the economy can grow over the long run, alongside slower productivity growth.

threads.title: A very open, export-led economy
threads.text: Sweden trades far more with the world than it did in the 1980s, across a wide range of products and markets. The IMF says high uncertainty and a tougher world economy are set to test this export-oriented economy.

growth_story.tension: The IMF calls Sweden a strong and resilient economy with some of the highest output per worker in Europe. Yet income per person has grown only 0.6 percent a year since 2008, and over 2016–2025 it ranked 9 of 11 among structural peers. The IMF also describes a moderate recovery in 2024, but income per person grew just 0.7 percent that year after falling 0.7 percent in 2023. The IMF's figures for the whole economy are higher, because the population kept rising.
